options.text: Whether the tests would catch small injected bugs (mutants)

questions.explanation: It injects small code changes and checks if any test fails, directly measuring whether tests would notice a bug.

questions.prompt: A mutant 'survives'. What does that mean?

options.text: A test failed, catching the injected bug
All tests still passed despite the injected bug — a gap in the tests

questions.explanation: A surviving mutant means the tests didn't notice the change — usually a missing or weak assertion or an untested case.

questions.prompt: A code change that doesn't alter observable behavior, so no test can kill it, is called an ____ mutant.
questions.explanation: Equivalent mutants survive without indicating weak tests, which is why a perfect mutation score is usually impractical.

questions.prompt: Why is mutation testing a stronger signal than coverage? Select all that apply.

options.text: It exercises whether results are actually asserted, not just executed
Each survivor is an actionable gap (missing assertion or case)
It is faster than a normal test run
A line can be 100% covered yet let a mutant survive

questions.explanation: Mutation testing checks assertion quality and yields actionable survivors; it is slower, not faster, than a normal run.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a mutation-testing run.

items.text: Run the test suite against each mutant
Classify killed vs survived and compute the mutation score

questions.explanation: Generate mutants, run tests against each, then tally killed/survived (ignoring equivalents) for the score.

questions.prompt: Match each mutation-testing term to its meaning.

pairs.right: A test failed, catching the change

questions.explanation: These terms describe the mechanics: mutants, kills, the score, and a common Python tool.
